about: The questions people ask first, each with a short answer and where to go next.

rows.title: How do I install NuclearLang?
rows.summary: One command installs the release of your system: `curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh | sh` on Linux and macOS, `irm https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows. At its end it offers the set-up of the AI services (the Smart Graph, the local agents and the models that fit your machine); `--no-ai` skips it.
body: ```sh
curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh | sh        # Linux and macOS
irm https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.ps1 | iex             # Windows (PowerShell)
It brings `nuclear`, `dragonfly`, the language server and `nuclear-loop`, with the dialects and type definitions, into your user folders. No Rust needed.

From the source tree: `./install.sh` builds and installs everything and the VS Code and Zed extensions (it needs Rust; `--no-vscode`, `--no-zed`, `--uninstall`). `./install.sh --ai` then runs the set-up of the AI services over the tree's own folders.
Then check the machine: `dragonfly doctor` says what is missing. For mobile apps, `dragonfly setup` installs Flutter step by step.

rows.title: How do I start a project?
rows.summary: `dragonfly new <name> -p backend` (or `-p mobile`, `-p web`) makes a project of `.nuc` files; `-d` picks a dialect. Then `dragonfly build`, `dragonfly install`, `dragonfly run` and `dragonfly test`.
body: ```sh
dragonfly new tasks_api -p backend            # a backend (fastapi; -d nestjs for TypeScript)
dragonfly new tasks_app                       # a mobile app (flutter)
dragonfly new site -p web                     # a web app (react)
cd tasks_api
dragonfly build && dragonfly install          # transpile, then the runtime and the packages
dragonfly test                                # the tests written in Nuclear
dragonfly run                                 # the server, or the app on a device

Then add what the product needs, generators first: `dragonfly gen resource <component> <Name> --fields "id:int name:string"` writes a whole resource; `dragonfly make <kind> <component> <Name>` writes one file of a kind. `nuclear check .` (or `dragonfly check`) reports every error.
For an AI agent working in the project: `dragonfly agent init` writes its `AGENTS.md` and the check hook.

rows.title: Which models do the local agents use, and can I change them?
rows.summary: On Ollama, by the profile the set-up installed. `hard`: `qwen2.5-coder:3b` writes code and `gemma4:e2b` plans, reviews and answers; `medium`: `qwen2.5-coder:3b`; `lite`: `qwen2.5-coder:1.5b`. `embeddinggemma` makes the graph's vectors in all three. None is larger than 3B parameters of effective size, and no GPU is needed.
body: - Which set a machine gets: `nuclear-loop setup` suggests one for its memory and disk (`concept:ai-setup` has what each downloads and how far it works); `nuclear-loop setup --status` says which one is installed.
- Another profile: run the set-up again. One model by hand: `CODER_MODEL`, `ASSISTANT_MODEL` and `NUCLEAR_GRAPH_EMBED` in `~/.config/nuclearlang/ai.env`, then restart the services.
- In VS Code: the *Settings and integrations* page (`Ctrl+Alt+S`) lists the Ollama models under the 3B rule, pulls one and restarts the services with it.
- A model over 3B parameters is not accepted: the agents are built for small models (fixed steps, the graph as memory, the compiler as judge).
- Without a GPU an answer takes from seconds to a few minutes; Ollama uses a GPU when the machine has one.

rows.title: Is my code sent anywhere?
rows.summary: No. The models run on Ollama on your machine, and the Smart Graph and the Nuclear Developer listen on `127.0.0.1` only. Something leaves the machine only when you choose it: a frontier model that leads, a spec imported from Jira or GitHub, an API read for its fields, a web search, a deploy.
body: - The graph refuses web pages (any request with an `Origin` header), gives nothing without a token you allowed (`nuclear-graph connect`, `allow`), and stores its texts encrypted (AES-256-GCM, the key in your keyring).
- `web_read` never reads a page of this machine or of the local network.
- With *Local agents only* (`--lead local`) a run needs no internet at all, unless its spec names an API to read.
- With *Claude leads*, the spec, the journal and the files Claude reads go to Anthropic through Claude Code, as with any Claude Code session.

rows.title: Where is the generated code, and can I edit it?
rows.summary:
The generated project is in `build/` (`build/app` for a mobile or web app). It is written again on every build, so it is never edited: change the `.nuc` files. To see what a piece becomes, `nuclear build --platform

` prints it.
body: - `dragonfly build` (or `nuclear build .`) writes `build/`: the target's sources, its manifest with only the packages of the enabled plugins, the wiring and the tests.
- Debugging works on the `.nuc` lines: the build keeps a line map, and `dragonfly explain` tells a run-time error or a test failure at its Nuclear lines.
- When something in the generated code looks wrong, it is a bug of the dialect or a value without a type in the `.nuc`: fix the source or report it; a hand edit is lost on the next build.

rows.title: How do I ask the local agent to do something?
rows.summary: In VS Code open the chat (`Ctrl+Alt+A`): a question is answered from the project's map and the Smart Graph; `/task <what to do>` is an order, run as a Loop by the local agents. For a whole feature write a spec (`Ctrl+Alt+P`) with its acceptance criteria.
body: - **A question** ("what does `BooksAppComponent` expose?", "how do I add a route?"): the assistant answers and changes nothing.
- **An order** (`/task add a use case that lists the books of an author`): a run of the Loop with the local agents; its journal says what was done.

- **A feature**: the Loop's spec page. Name each piece with the platform's words (a model `Book`, a repository `BookRepository`, a use case `ListBooks`) and add one acceptance criterion per behaviour. For a resource of an API, add its `GET <url>` line or an example answer and the generators write it.
- **From a terminal**: `nuclear-loop run specs/<id>/spec.md --lead local`.
- **From Claude Code, Codex or Cursor**: the MCP tool `developer_task`.
The agent tells you when a task is beyond it; then let a frontier model lead or split the task.

rows.title: Which languages and frameworks does NuclearLang produce?
rows.summary: TypeScript, Dart and Python as plain languages; and through Dragonfly: FastAPI (Python) or NestJS (TypeScript) for a backend, Flutter (Dart) for a mobile app, React (TypeScript) for a web app.
body: | You write | Dialect | Comes out |
| the base language | `typescript`, `dart`, `python` | a program in that language |
| the backend platform | `fastapi` | a Python service |
| the backend platform | `nestjs` | a TypeScript service |
| the mobile platform | `flutter` | a Flutter app: Android, iOS, desktop, web |
| the web platform | `react` | a React web app |
Node.js with Express is postponed. A new target is a new dialect, made of data files.

rows.title: How do I learn the syntax quickly?
rows.summary:
Read the short sheet: `nuclear spec --brief` (the base language) and `nuclear spec --brief --platform backend|mobile|web`. For one topic, `nuclear help `; for a kind or decorator, `nuclear help --platform

`. The compiler corrects the habits of other languages with exact fixes.
body: The ten things that differ from TypeScript, Dart or Python:
1. Blocks by indentation of 2 spaces; no braces, no semicolons.
2. The type goes after the name: `name: string`, `f(a: int) string`.
3. The last line of a function is its value; `return` only leaves early.
4. `x = 1` declares; no `const`, `let`, `var`, `final`.
5. `User("Ana")` constructs; no `new`. Named arguments use `=`: `f(name = "Ana")`.
6. `~load()` awaits; no `await`, no `async`.
7. `and`, `or`, `not`; `x in xs` for membership.
8. `if` and `match` are values.
9. `"Hi ${name}"` interpolates in every string; comments are `//`.
10. No imports: the names of the target's libraries are imported by themselves.
Then write, run `nuclear check <file> --json`, and apply what each error says (`nuclear fix` applies the exact ones).
